summary:
This run covered 9 evals, but data is sparse and uneven between variants: for most evals, only one of the two variants has results recorded (the other is null), meaning direct head-to-head comparison is only possible for 3 of the 9 evals (ac-oauth-claim-mismatch, ac-obs-transaction-search, and partially bedrock-agent-empty-response which has only without_skill data). Two evals (neg-kb-ingestion-zero-docs, neg-token-quota-throttle) were skipped entirely because they are "should_trigger: false" negative tests — both variants correctly did not fire the trigger, which is expected behavior, not a weakness.

Where only one variant has data, those results describe that variant alone and say nothing about the other:
- bedrock-agent-empty-response: only without_skill ran. It failed its expected-output check (0/1) and passed 4/6 assertions, failing on "finding carries severity/concrete signal" and "names an AGT/AC catalog check-id."
- agentcore-runtime-cannot-invoke, ac-gateway-tool-schema, ac-scp-explicit-deny, ac-memory-not-persisting: only with_skill ran. In three of these (agentcore-runtime-cannot-invoke, ac-scp-explicit-deny, ac-memory-not-persisting) with_skill passed all assertions and met expected output (though agentcore-runtime-cannot-invoke's expected_output percentage is oddly listed as 0/1 despite 5/5 assertions passing — worth flagging as a possible scoring inconsistency). In ac-gateway-tool-schema, with_skill passed 3/4 assertions, failing the "no raw 12-digit account ID exposed" check — a concrete leak that needs attention regardless of variant.

For the two evals with direct pairwise comparison:
- ac-oauth-claim-mismatch: both variants met expected output and passed all 5/5 assertions — every assertion passed for both variants, so none of them differentiate the variants here. On quality, without_skill was favored on actionability and completeness (accuracy was comparable), with medium confidence. without_skill also ran faster (18s vs 27s) and cheaper ($0.15 vs $0.23).
- ac-obs-transaction-search: both variants again passed all 5/5 assertions (fully overlapping, non-differentiating). Quality comparison favored with_skill on all three criteria (accuracy, actionability, completeness) with high confidence. Runtime and cost were nearly identical (21s/$0.18 vs 22s/$0.18).

So in the only two cases allowing direct comparison, quality favored different variants in each case (without_skill in one, with_skill in the other), both times on top of identical assertion pass rates, and runtime/cost differences were small and not consistently favoring either side.

No output-consistency data (run-to-run variation) was available for any eval on either variant, so stability across repeated runs cannot be assessed here. Confidence in the quality-comparison findings is medium in one case and high in the other, but these rest on a single pair each, so the sample size is very small. Overall, the dataset is too fragmented — with most evals having only one variant's results — to draw a broad comparative conclusion; the few direct comparisons available show mixed, modest differences in quality with no clear consistent pattern, alongside a couple of flagged issues (an account-ID leak in one with_skill run, an apparent expected-output/assertion scoring mismatch in another) that merit review independent of the variant comparison.

Note: a DevOps Agent endpoint outage failed some runs in this pass. Those scenarios (ac-gateway-tool-schema, ac-memory-not-persisting, ac-scp-explicit-deny, agentcore-runtime-cannot-invoke, bedrock-agent-empty-response) were rerun on the same agent spaces with the same settings, and their results replace the failed runs.

bedrock-agent-empty-response.summary:
Both variants were evaluated on a single chat task. The trigger behavior under test fired successfully (1/1).

Expected output: Neither variant met the expected output (0/1 for both). Variant_a's failure judgment was made with high confidence, while without_skill's was made with medium confidence, meaning the "miss" verdict for without_skill rests on a somewhat weaker judgment than for with_skill. Still, both are recorded as not meeting expectations.

Assertions: Both variants had identical assertion pass rates (4/6, 67%), and critically, the pattern was the same across every individual assertion — there were no cases where one variant passed and the other failed. Three assertions passed for both (resolving the agent alias before concluding what's live, checking guardrail attachment, and naming concrete ordered checks rather than generic advice; also the check that no raw 12-digit account ID is exposed passed for both). Two assertions failed for both variants: one requiring that each finding carry a severity and a concrete supporting signal (medium confidence for with_skill's failure, high confidence for without_skill's), and a regex check requiring at least one finding to carry an AGT/AC catalog check-id. Since these two assertions failed identically for both variants, they point to a shared gap in behavior (or a possibly overly strict assertion) rather than a difference between the variants.

Performance: Variant_a ran slower (~33s vs ~14s, about 19s more) and cost more (~$0.28 vs ~$0.12, roughly 2.3x). Context window utilization was similar and low for both (5.2% vs 4.8%), with no compactions for either. These metrics show without_skill completing the task faster and cheaper on this single run, but since expected-output and assertion results are essentially tied, this is a runtime/cost difference rather than evidence of a quality gap.

Quality comparison and consistency: No quality pairs could be evaluated (0 evaluated, 1 skipped), so there is no direct quality-comparison data between the variants. Output consistency across repeated runs was not available (null) for both variants, so repeatability cannot be assessed from this data.

Overall, this is based on a single task instance, which limits how much can be generalized. On the measured assertions, the two variants performed identically — same passes, same failures — and both failed to meet the expected output (with differing confidence levels behind that call). The main observed difference is that without_skill ran faster and at lower cost than with_skill in this instance, while no quality-comparison or consistency data exists to weigh against that difference.

agentcore-runtime-cannot-invoke.summary:
Both variants were run on a single chat task about diagnosing a Bedrock permissions issue, and the trigger for the test fired as expected.

Expected-output match: both with_skill and without_skill failed the overall expected-output check (0/1), each with high-confidence judgments. So on this top-line measure, neither variant met the bar, and that failure is a well-supported (high-confidence) finding rather than a borderline call.

Assertion-level detail (this is where the two variants diverge sharply): with_skill passed 4 of 5 assertions, without_skill passed 0 of 5. The breakdown matters:
- Three content/reasoning assertions (inspecting the execution role rather than guessing, correctly identifying the missing bedrock:InvokeModel permission as the cause, and framing the fix as something for the operator to apply rather than claiming to have applied it) were passed by with_skill and failed by without_skill, all with high-confidence LLM judgments.
- One regex check (naming an LLM-AC check-id) was likewise passed by with_skill and failed by without_skill.
- One regex check (avoiding exposure of a raw 12-digit account ID) failed for both variants — this assertion is not distinguishing the two systems; it points to a shared weakness (or an overly strict check) rather than a difference between them.

So despite both variants failing the overall expected_output gate, the per-assertion data shows with_skill satisfied most of the individual criteria while without_skill satisfied none, with the sole shared failure being the account-ID exposure check.

Performance and cost: with_skill took about 52s and cost about $0.43 on average, while without_skill was faster and cheaper at about 24s and $0.21. Context-window utilization was low for both (6.0% vs 4.7%) with no compaction events. This is a real tradeoff: without_skill is roughly twice as fast and half the cost, but with_skill produced substantially more assertion passes on this task.

Quality comparison and consistency: no quality pairs could be evaluated (0 evaluated, 1 skipped), so there is no direct pairwise quality judgment to weigh in. Output consistency across repeated runs is not available for either variant (null), so run-to-run stability cannot be assessed here.

Overall, this is a single-task, low-sample result: the only hard, high-confidence finding is that both variants failed the explicit expected-output check, and that both failed the account-ID-exposure assertion. Beyond that, with_skill showed clearly stronger per-assertion performance on this task while without_skill was notably faster and cheaper — a speed/cost vs. assertion-pass-rate tradeoff rather than a clear overall verdict, and with no quality-comparison or consistency data to corroborate either direction.

ac-oauth-claim-mismatch.summary:
Both variants fully met the expected output (1/1) and passed all 5 assertions (5/5), on a single evaluated task/pair, so this is a very small sample and conclusions should be treated as directional rather than robust.

Assertion-level detail: all five assertions passed for both variants with the same pattern ("always_passes"), meaning none of the assertions in this eval actually differentiated the variants — they show both agents correctly read the runtime's inbound JWT authorizer config, identified the client ID mismatch, distinguished a config issue from a token validity issue, framed the fix as an operator action without falsely claiming to have made the change, and avoided exposing a raw account ID. Confidence on these assertion judgments was high for with_skill across the board, and high for without_skill on four of five, with one (reading the authorizer config) rated medium confidence for without_skill — a minor weak point in that specific measurement, not a failure.

On the single pairwise quality comparison available, without_skill was favored overall (2 criteria favored vs 0 for with_skill, with 1 marked comparable). Breaking this down: "accuracy" was rated comparable (no difference), while "actionability" and "completeness" were each favored toward without_skill. This comparison carries only medium average confidence and is based on just one evaluated pair, so it should be read as a mild, low-certainty signal rather than a strong differentiator.

On efficiency metrics, without_skill ran faster (~18s vs ~27s, a ~9s difference) and cost less (~$0.15 vs ~$0.23) than with_skill. Context window utilization was low and similar for both (4.7% vs 5.1%), with no compaction events for either. Neither variant exceeded the 30s runtime threshold in the runtime comparison (1 pair evaluated).

Output consistency across repeated runs was not available (null) for either variant, so nothing can be said about run-to-run stability for either agent.

Overall, this is a single-task, high-pass-rate eval where both variants performed equivalently on correctness and assertions, with a mild, lower-confidence quality edge and a clearer runtime/cost edge favoring without_skill. Given the very limited sample (one task, one pairwise comparison) and lack of consistency data, these results should be seen as a narrow snapshot rather than a definitive comparison.

Overall, this single task shows both variants succeeding equally on correctness-style checks (trigger, expected output, assertions), while without_skill was faster, cheaper, and favored in the one quality comparison available — a pattern worth noting but based on a small sample (one task, one quality pair) rather than a broad, high-confidence trend.

ac-scp-explicit-deny.summary:
This evaluation covers a single chat task involving diagnosing an IAM-style explicit deny issue, with only one test pair evaluated per variant, so findings here rest on limited data and should be read as indicative rather than conclusive.

Trigger and expected output: The behavior under test fired as expected (1/1), and both with_skill and without_skill fully met the expected output (1/1, 100%) with high confidence on that judgment — a strong, non-differentiating result in both cases.

Assertions: All 4 assertions passed for both variants (4/4, 100% each), and every individual assertion (identifying the deny source, explaining deny-overrides-allow, giving a concrete way to find the responsible policy, and not exposing a raw account ID) passed for both variants. Because every assertion passed for both, none of them differentiate the variants — they indicate the underlying task and checks were handled correctly by both, but the assertion set doesn't reveal any contrast.

Quality comparison: Looking at the one evaluated pair, with_skill was favored overall in 2 aspects with 1 rated comparable (no pairs favored without_skill). Breaking this down by criterion: accuracy was rated comparable between the two; actionability and completeness were each rated in favor of with_skill. This comparison carries only medium average confidence and is based on a single pair, so it should be treated as a modest, not strong, signal favoring with_skill's output richness in this one instance.

Runtime and cost: with_skill took about 31 seconds and cost roughly $0.26 per run, while without_skill was recorded at 0 seconds and $0.00 cost. The single runtime comparison pair flagged this run as exceeding the 30-second threshold (high confidence), which aligns with with_skill's ~31s runtime. Variant_b's 0s/$0.00 figures suggest it may not have incurred the same metered cost/runtime in this case — this is a notable asymmetry worth flagging rather than treating as a straightforward 'faster/cheaper' win, since it may reflect a difference in how the run was executed or measured rather than a comparable apples-to-apples cost tradeoff.

Context window utilization was low and similar for both (with_skill 4.9%, without_skill 4.4%), with no compactions for either — no meaningful difference here.

Output consistency: No consistency data was available for either variant (both null), so repeat-run stability could not be assessed in this evaluation.

Overall, this is a single-pair, low-volume comparison where both variants satisfied the explicit pass/fail checks equally, with a modest, medium-confidence quality edge toward with_skill's actionability and completeness, set against a large runtime/cost difference whose measurement basis for without_skill is unclear. Given the small sample (one pair) and lack of consistency data, these results should be treated as a limited snapshot rather than a definitive comparison.

ac-obs-transaction-search.summary:
This evaluation covered a single chat task about diagnosing missing CloudWatch Transaction Search / OpenTelemetry instrumentation issues, and the trigger behavior under test fired successfully.

Both variants met the expected output in full (1/1, high confidence for both), and both passed all 5 assertions (100%), with high confidence on the 4 LLM-graded assertions and a clean pass on the regex check for not exposing a raw account ID. Because every assertion passed identically for both variants, none of these individual checks differentiate the two systems — they confirm both handled the core task requirements (explaining the two root causes, the correlation problem, giving operator-facing steps without claiming to have made changes, and avoiding sensitive data exposure) equally well. This being based on a single task/pair means the measurements, while high-confidence, reflect only one scenario rather than a broad sample.

Runtime and cost were nearly identical: with_skill averaged 22s vs without_skill's 21s (a negligible ~1s difference), and both cost $0.18 on average. Context window utilization was low for both (5.6% vs 4.3%), with no compaction needed in either case — not a meaningful differentiator. Neither run exceeded the 30s runtime threshold.

The one dimension showing a difference is output quality: in the single pair evaluated, with_skill was favored over without_skill across all three quality criteria (accuracy, actionability, completeness), with high average confidence in that judgment. However, this is based on only one evaluated pair, so it should be read as a signal from a single comparison rather than a robustly replicated pattern.

Output consistency (variation across repeated runs) was not available for either variant (marked null), so we cannot speak to run-to-run stability for either system in this evaluation.

Overall: on correctness (expected output and assertions), the two variants performed identically and at a high standard. The only distinguishing signal is a quality-criteria preference for with_skill in the single pair assessed, alongside essentially equivalent runtime, cost, and resource usage. Given the single-task sample size and lack of consistency data, this should be treated as a limited, single-instance observation rather than a definitive quality gap.

This evaluation covers a single chat task about AgentCore memory/session handling. The triggering behavior fired as expected (1/1).

Both with_skill and without_skill fully met the expected output (1/1, high confidence for both), and both passed all 4 assertions (100%). Notably, every individual assertion — checking that memory/session/actor identifiers are passed on invocation, that read/write permissions are considered, that the response distinguishes 'not written' from 'not retrieved' memory issues, and that no raw 12-digit account ID is exposed — passed for both variants identically. Since all assertions passed for both, none of them differentiate the two variants; the task's core correctness bar was equally met by both.

On cost and runtime, the two variants were essentially tied: both averaged ~14s runtime and ~$0.12 cost. Context window utilization was slightly lower for without_skill (4.7% vs 5.5%), with neither variant triggering any context compaction — a minor, likely inconsequential difference.

Where a difference does appear is in the side-by-side quality comparison, though this rests on just a single evaluated pair, so it should be treated as a limited, low-sample signal rather than a robust finding. Out of that one comparable pair, without_skill was favored on two sub-judgments (actionability and completeness) and the two were rated comparable on accuracy; with_skill was not favored on any criterion in this single comparison. The overall confidence for this quality judgment is medium, and with only one pair evaluated, this result should be weighed cautiously rather than treated as a decisive quality gap.

No output-consistency data was available for either variant (both null), so repeat-run stability could not be assessed for either side.

Overall, this is a case where the measured correctness dimensions (expected output, assertions, trigger) show no difference between with_skill and without_skill — both performed identically and fully met requirements — while a single, medium-confidence quality comparison leans toward without_skill on actionability and completeness. Runtime and cost were effectively equivalent. Given the very small sample (one task, one quality pair) and lack of consistency data, this should be read as a tentative, low-volume signal rather than a strong differentiator between the two variants.
